lead.eyebrow: Pre-OPEC+ Independence Day — Markets Dark, Riyadh Speaks Tomorrow: The $72 Recovery Buys Time but July 5 Defines the Floor
lead.headline: Brent Recovers to $72.30 on Iran Peace Optimism as OPEC+ July 5 Ministerial Looms — US Markets Dark for Independence Day, Global Eyes on Saudi Signal
paragraphs: Oil markets ended the pre-holiday session Friday with a modest but meaningful recovery: Brent added $0.43 to close at $72.30 and WTI ticked up to $69.00 as traders cautiously bet that peace efforts between the United States and Iran would hold, following President Trump's statement Thursday that US-Iran negotiations were "progressing well" after Qatari and Pakistani mediators met both sides in Doha on July 2. The uptick — small in percentage terms — is strategically significant: it came off the $70.89 close on July 2 that had been threatening to crack the Saudi fiscal breakeven floor, and it arrived in a pre-holiday tape with thin volume. Now, with US markets dark for Independence Day, the global oil market is effectively frozen in anticipation of tomorrow's event that matters more than anything in the past month.

That event is the OPEC+ July 5 ministerial. The seven-member group — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — approved a fourth consecutive monthly output increase of 188,000 bpd for July when they last met June 7. The August decision now pending is different in kind from its predecessors: with Brent having tested $70 this week and Riyadh's estimated fiscal breakeven at $70–$75 per barrel, the market-share versus price-defense calculus Saudi Arabia has navigated since the Hormuz reopening is at its most acute inflection point. The approximately 67 million barrels of Iranian floating storage unlocking under Treasury's 60-day sanctions waiver are suppressing prices from above; the EIA's fourth consecutive crude draw is failing to provide the floor it would historically deliver. Riyadh needs to decide, before the August data gets worse, whether it will defend the floor or cede it to Iranian supply normalization.

The backdrop for tomorrow's ministerial is a market with two competing gravity fields: Iranian supply normalization that is bearish on any forward-price baseline, and a Saudi fiscal arithmetic that is approaching a line that historically triggers production discipline signals. Friday's peace-optimism recovery to $72.30 is not a resolution of that tension — it is the market buying time before tomorrow. The signal that matters is not what OPEC+ formally decides at the July 5 meeting; formal decisions take weeks to move supply. The signal is what Saudi Arabia says about the pace of further increases, and whether the word "pause" appears in any form in the post-meeting communiqué. A Saudi production-pause signal — which costs Riyadh nothing except the psychological concession of stepping back from the market-share posture — has historically been worth $3–5 per barrel on its own. That signal, or its conspicuous absence, is what oil markets will be pricing the morning of July 6.

news.headline: Trump: US-Iran Negotiations 'Progressing Well' as Doha Mediation Holds — Brent Bounces to $72.30
news.body: President Trump said Thursday that US-Iran negotiations toward a permanent peace settlement were "progressing well" following a July 2 mediation session in Doha involving Qatari and Pakistani envoys who met with both American and Iranian delegations. The statement lifted crude in pre-holiday trading on July 3: Brent added $0.43 to close at $72.30 and WTI moved to $69.00 — a directionally significant recovery off the $70.89 Brent close Wednesday that had been approaching the Saudi fiscal breakeven floor. Phase-2 negotiations in Geneva continue on three unresolved pillars from the June 17 MOU: IAEA inspection access, Iranian reconstruction funding, and permanent ceasefire architecture. A framework IAEA agreement before July 12 would substantially reduce the market's largest remaining upside risk — the August 21 waiver-lapse scenario — which is currently priced at near-zero probability.

news.headline: OPEC+ July 5: Four Consecutive 188k bpd Hikes in the Rearview — Will Riyadh Signal a Pause as Brent Tests Fiscal Floor?
news.body: The OPEC+ ministerial convening tomorrow is the group's most consequential scheduled event since the first post-war output decision in May. Seven core producers — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — have approved four consecutive monthly increases of 188,000 bpd each since the Strait of Hormuz began reopening. The fifth decision, covering August output, arrives with Brent at $72.30 — approaching the Saudi fiscal breakeven of $70–$75/bbl. Saudi Arabia's $6 per barrel July Arab Light OSP cut signaled market-share retention as the priority. The question for July 5 is whether approaching the fiscal floor changes that calculus. The group reaffirmed "full flexibility to increase, pause or reverse" the phase-out — an escape clause Riyadh may need to invoke before the August EIA inventory build from Gulf crude arrives in late July.

news.headline: UAE Exports Return to Pre-War Levels Using Fujairah Bypass and Dark Tankers — Saudi Still 25% Below Pre-War
news.body: The UAE has restored oil exports to approximately 3.9 million bpd — close to pre-war levels — using a combination of the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline's Fujairah bypass route and dark tanker operations, according to Bloomberg reporting from July 1. The Fujairah bypass allows UAE crude to reach the Gulf of Oman without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi exports remain approximately 25% below pre-war rates; Iraq has recovered to 1.76 mb/d in June from 1.49 mb/d in April. Total Hormuz flows have crossed 10 mb/d with US military confirmation, but remain well below the pre-war baseline of 18–20 mb/d. The UAE's rapid export recovery — partly routed around the Strait entirely — highlights the asymmetry between producers with bypass infrastructure and those fully dependent on Hormuz normalization.

news.headline: Iraq Threatens OPEC Exit Over Quota Dispute — Baghdad's July 5 Posture Is a Cartel-Fragmentation Signal
news.body: Iraq — OPEC's second-largest producer — has signaled it may follow the UAE out of the cartel if its production quota is not significantly revised upward. Baghdad's long-term production target is 5 mb/d, with an eventual 7 mb/d export ambition, but actual post-war output runs near 1.76 mb/d as field damage suppresses production while quota frameworks remain calibrated to pre-war capacity. The UAE formally exited OPEC+ in May 2026 citing national interests; an Iraqi exit would remove the cartel's second-largest producer and accelerate the fragmentation eroding OPEC+'s pricing power. Iraq's participation and tone at tomorrow's July 5 ministerial is the near-term signal — a walkout or formal ultimatum would be a market-moving structural development independent of any price-floor decision.

news.headline: Fourth Consecutive US Crude Draw of 3.8M Bbl Fails to Arrest Decline — Gulf Crude Still 20–35 Days From US Ports
news.body: The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report for the week ending June 26, released July 1, confirmed a fourth consecutive US crude inventory draw of 3.8 million barrels, leaving commercial crude stocks at 408.4 million barrels — roughly 7% below the five-year seasonal average. Gasoline stocks drew 2.3 million barrels; distillates built 2.5 million barrels. Despite the sustained draw signal, data failed to provide a lasting price floor — WTI slid to a post-war low of $67.89 on July 2 before recovering on peace optimism July 3. The structural reason: Ras Tanura resumed VLCC loadings only in the final days of June, and those barrels require 20–35 days to reach US East Coast ports. The first EIA report to show Gulf crude arriving at scale — likely the July 16 or July 23 release — is the data event that will actually define the supply recovery narrative.

news.headline: Wood Mackenzie: Era of $2–$4 Henry Hub Is Ending — Structural Shift Toward $5/MMBtu Real by 2035
news.body: Wood Mackenzie published a July 2 analysis warning that the era of Henry Hub natural gas prices in the $2–$4/MMBtu range is ending as structural demand and supply conditions shift materially over the coming decade. The firm projects Henry Hub will reach $5/MMBtu in real terms by 2035, driven by surging LNG export demand, power sector gas consumption, and the difficulty of replicating Permian and Marcellus production economics that underpinned the current price regime. Henry Hub traded at $3.24/MMBtu on July 3, up 1.6% on the session — still within the low range Wood Mackenzie identifies as structurally unsustainable. For oil market participants, a sustained gas price repricing above $4–$5 would increase cross-fuel competition dynamics and alter refinery economics across the Atlantic Basin in the years ahead.

events.name: OPEC+ Ministerial — August Output Decision; Saudi Pause Signal or Market-Share Continuation
events.impact: The most consequential scheduled event in the near-term oil calendar. Seven OPEC+ producers must decide August output with Brent at $72.30 — approaching the Saudi fiscal breakeven of $70–$75/bbl. Four options are on the table: (1) A fifth consecutive 188,000 bpd increase — bearish, confirms market-share priority; (2) A production pause — the floor-defense signal markets are watching for; (3) A production cut — unlikely but maximally bullish; (4) A vague communiqué leaving all options open — bearish by ambiguity. Iraq's quota dispute and possible exit threat add a structural fragmentation dimension. The Saudi post-meeting statement — not the formal decision text but Riyadh's tone and framing — is historically worth $3–$5/bbl and will drive the July 6 open.
events.market_impact: Saudi signals production pause: $3–5/bbl rally; Brent tests $75–$77. Fifth increase approved, status quo: $1–2/bbl further softness; $70 floor tests resume. Saudi ambiguous or silent: $1/bbl softness; market interprets silence as market-share continuation.

events.name: Geneva Phase-2 IAEA Framework Agreement — Removes Last Major Upside Risk Before August 21
events.impact: Vice President Vance's Phase-2 Iran negotiations in Geneva continue on three unresolved MOU pillars: IAEA inspection access and frequency, Iranian reconstruction funding, and permanent ceasefire architecture. US officials describe progress as 'constructive but complex,' with preliminary agreement on the number of IAEA inspection sites but remaining disputes over access timelines and inspector credentials. A completed framework before July 12 would substantially reduce the probability of the August 21 waiver-lapse scenario — the single largest remaining upside catalyst in the market, currently priced at near-zero. A Geneva impasse or Iranian walkout would re-open that risk and represent a $5–8/bbl upside shock from current levels.
events.market_impact: IAEA framework agreed before July 12: removes largest upside risk; $1–2/bbl incrementally bearish. Geneva breakdown: $5–8/bbl spike; Iran supply re-constraint narrative re-enters market.

events.name: First EIA Report to Show Gulf Crude Arriving at US Ports — Supply Recovery Data Lands
events.impact: Ras Tanura resumed VLCC loadings in late June; those barrels are 20–35 transit days from US East Coast refineries. The EIA report covering the week ending July 11 (released July 16) or week ending July 18 (released July 23) will be the first to potentially register a material US crude build from Gulf supply. When that data arrives, the narrative shifts from residual domestic scarcity — sustained by four consecutive draws — to confirmed supply recovery. Four consecutive draws have provided a psychological floor in the $68–$70 range; when the first large Gulf-origin build appears, that floor disappears.
events.market_impact: Build >4M bbl confirming Gulf crude arrival: $2–3/bbl downward pressure; WTI tests $65–$66. Continued draw (delayed transit): residual scarcity floor preserved; support holds $68–$70.

events.name: Treasury Sanctions Waiver Expiry — Treaty, Extension, or Lapse Sets Iranian Crude's Permanent Market Status
events.impact: Treasury Secretary Bessent's 60-day sanctions waiver authorizing third-party purchases of Iranian crude runs through August 21 — approximately 47 days away. Three outcomes remain live: (1) Treaty signed before deadline — permanent sanctions removal, full Iranian crude market access, maximum bearish; (2) Waiver extended pending continued negotiations — status quo, incrementally bearish; (3) Waiver lapses without extension or treaty — sanctions re-impose, Iranian exports sharply curtailed, sharpest upside price shock remaining on the calendar. The market currently prices scenarios (1) or (2) as near-certainty; the probability assigned to a lapse is effectively zero — creating a significant asymmetric upside tail for any event that raises that probability.
events.market_impact: Treaty signed or waiver extended: bearish status quo; Iranian supply recovery continues uninterrupted. Waiver lapses without extension: $5–8/bbl spike; 2–3 week sustained rally.

events.name: Iraq OPEC Exit Negotiations — Quota Dispute Threatens Cartel's Second-Largest Producer
events.impact: Iraq's quota grievances — producing ~1.76 mb/d against a capacity-based quota of 4.378 mb/d — create structural tension that tomorrow's July 5 ministerial must address or defer. An exit does not produce barrels tomorrow — war-damaged fields limit actual output for months — but sets a structural path toward unconstrained Iraqi supply growth that is incrementally bearish over a 12–24 month horizon. The UAE's May exit established the precedent; a second defection would signal cartel fragmentation that outlasts the current Hormuz crisis. Iraq's participation and tone at July 5 is the near-term signal: a walkout or formal ultimatum would be market-moving independent of any price-floor decision.
events.market_impact: Iraq exits OPEC+: medium-term bearish structural signal; no immediate supply addition while damage is repaired. Iraq secures expanded quota at July 5: near-term neutral; supply growth contained within cartel framework.

paragraphs: US markets are dark today. The NYMEX is quiet for Independence Day. And yet the global oil market is anything but still — it is holding its breath ahead of the single most consequential event on its near-term calendar: tomorrow's OPEC+ July 5 ministerial, where Saudi Arabia must decide, in the presence of a restless Iraq and an accelerating Iranian supply surge, whether to defend the $70 floor or concede it to the physics of post-war normalization. Friday's modest Brent recovery to $72.30 is not a resolution of this tension. It is the last price the market set before it learns what Riyadh intends to do.

My read going into July 5: The case for a Saudi production pause signal is stronger today than it was two weeks ago. Brent at $70.89 on Thursday crossed within dollars of the fiscal breakeven. The July 3 recovery was thin-volume, pre-holiday, and catalyzed by Trump's "progressing well" comment on Iran talks — not by any fundamental change in the supply picture. Iranian floating storage is day 12 of its 60-day unlock. The market is still a month from seeing Gulf crude arrive in US EIA data. If Riyadh stays silent through July 5 — or worse, approves a fifth consecutive increase — it signals that the Kingdom has made peace with sub-$72 oil as the price of Hormuz normalization, and the next stop is the mid-$60s. A pause signal does not require an emergency meeting or a formal cut; a single well-sourced paragraph from Riyadh after the ministerial changes everything.

The structural picture: We are approximately 47 days from August 21 — the Treasury sanctions waiver expiry that is either a date on a calendar or the most important binary oil market event of the year, depending on whether Geneva delivers a treaty. The market has priced waiver lapse at essentially zero. That zero-pricing is correct in expectation but dangerous in concentration: any development that raises the lapse probability even marginally will produce a disproportionate price response from a tape that carries no geopolitical premium whatsoever. A Hormuz mine incident, a Geneva walkout, an Iraqi OPEC exit at the July 5 meeting — any of these would hit a market that has assumed away every remaining tail risk. The asymmetry is the defining feature of the July 2026 oil market: the downside is gradual and well-understood; the upside is discontinuous and unpriced.

My call: Brent $70–$75 into and after July 5, with the outcome of tomorrow's ministerial determining which end of the range the next week trades. Saudi pause signal: Brent $73–$76. Saudi silence or fifth hike: Brent $68–$70, $70 floor tests resume. The floor is not broken yet — but it requires Riyadh to defend it. Four consecutive draws haven't done it on their own. Peace optimism hasn't done it either. The only thing that reliably anchors Brent above $70 from here is OPEC+ pricing discipline, and tomorrow is the moment Riyadh signals which side of that choice it is on. Everything else is noise until July 6 morning.
